summary: The MIKEY key management scheme's existing modes do not suit deployments with a centralized key management service. This document defines new ticket-based MIKEY modes for those deployments. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Instead of each pair of phones working out keys alone, a central office gives out tickets that let them set up shared keys quickly.

questions: how does mikey use a key management service
what is key forking in mikey
what are the mikey ticket modes
subtitle: Adds Kerberos-style tickets to MIKEY so a central key management service can hand out media session keys.

tldr.problem: The existing MIKEY modes rely on peers negotiating directly or on pre-distributed credentials, which suits neither large deployments with a central key service nor calls that are forked to several devices.
tldr.mechanism: MIKEY-TICKET lets an Initiator get keys and a ticket from a Key Management Service (KMS), send the ticket to the Responder, and let the Responder have the KMS resolve it into keys. Up to three round trips are used, and some can be skipped depending on the ticket type.
tldr.outcome: It gives a flexible framework with a default MIKEY base ticket, optional key forking and new 256-bit algorithms. The RFC is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6309.

facts.label: Exchanges
facts.value: Ticket Request, Ticket Transfer, Ticket Resolve

facts.label: Modes
facts.value: 4, by who holds the ticket protection key

today: RFC 6043 is an Informational RFC and has been updated by RFC 6309. It was not obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Ticket Mode for MIKEY
sections.content:
Key management is based on direct negotiation between peers (such as Diffie-Hellman), on pre-distributed credentials, or on a trusted Key Management Service (KMS). The Multimedia Internet KEYing (MIKEY) modes in RFC 3830 and its extensions are variants of the first two.

With a KMS, users request credentials when needed instead of having them pre-distributed, and the approach scales well as the number of users grows. MIKEY-TICKET adds a set of modes built on a ticket concept similar to Kerberos (RFC 4120). It is designed mainly for media plane security in the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS).
sections.eli5: Big organizations prefer one trusted office that hands out keys on request. MIKEY-TICKET teaches MIKEY to work that way.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.content:
A request may be delivered to several endpoints, called forking: several devices of one user, or a group address where only one person should answer. If all endpoints share one pre-shared key, each of them can read the session keys. If each has its own key, the Initiator does not know which one to use. So the ticket is not bound to the exact Responder until that Responder is known.

The ticket can hold a reference to keys stored at the KMS, or hold the keys itself, in which case it must be confidentiality and integrity protected. The RFC also warns that a central KMS may be a single point of security failure, so its security requirements may be about those of an AAA server or a Certification Authority. The mechanism also supports group key management and deferred delivery to users who are offline.
sections.eli5: If one phone call rings on three phones, only the one that picks up should learn the secret. A ticket lets the office decide at the last moment who gets it.

sections.title: Three Parties and Four Modes
sections.content:
Earlier MIKEY modes were a single or half round trip between two peers. MIKEY-TICKET involves three parties (Initiator, Responder and KMS) and up to three round trips: Ticket Request (Initiator and KMS), Ticket Transfer (Initiator and Responder) and Ticket Resolve (Responder and KMS). Request and Resolve are meant to be used with Transfer, not alone. The KMS takes no part in the media session itself.

Which exchanges are needed depends on who can open the ticket. If only the KMS knows the protecting key, all three are used (mode 1). If it is shared between the KMS and the Responder, Resolve is omitted (mode 2). If it is shared between the Initiator and the KMS, Request is omitted (mode 3). If it is shared between Initiator and Responder, both are omitted (mode 4).
sections.eli5: Sometimes the helper office must be asked twice, sometimes once, and sometimes not at all, depending on who already holds the secret lock key.

sections.title: The Exchanges and Messages
sections.content:
In the full mode the Initiator sends REQUEST_INIT to the KMS, integrity protected by a MAC from a pre-shared key or by a signature. The KMS returns REQUEST_RESP with the keys and a ticket. The Initiator sends the ticket in TRANSFER_INIT, protected by a MAC based on a MIKEY Protection Key (MPK) encoded in the ticket.

If the Responder accepts the Ticket Policy and session security policies, it sends RESOLVE_INIT to the KMS, which checks authorization and returns the keys in RESOLVE_RESP. With key forking, the KMS modifies the keys to bind them to that Responder. The Responder then sends TRANSFER_RESP to the Initiator as verification. Tickets may be reused, so a single Ticket Request can be followed by several Ticket Transfers. The default ticket type is the MIKEY base ticket (Appendix A of the RFC). The RFC also defines the GENERIC-ID map type to remove the limits of the SRTP-ID map type.
sections.eli5: The first friend asks the office for a ticket, passes it on, and the second friend shows it to the office to get the secret. Then the second friend tells the first it worked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the many optional features add complexity, and strongly encourages protocol designers to define strict profiles of the options. All keys, including those protecting tickets, MUST be 128 bits or more. Random nonces in key derivation counter offline pre-computation attacks, and the combined RANDRi and RANDRr lengths MUST at least equal the longest pre-shared key, envelope key, MPK, TGK or GTGK.

The new algorithms PRF-HMAC-SHA-256, AES-CM-256 and HMAC-SHA-256-256 use 256-bit keys. If one is supported, the other two SHALL be supported too, and they SHALL NOT be mixed with algorithms using smaller keys. Without key forking, anyone who can resolve the ticket gets the keys; with forking, the master TGKs are known only to the Initiator and KMS. The KMS builds no protocol state before authenticating a party, timestamps and a replay cache stop replay of whole messages, and rate-limiting and ACLs SHOULD be used against denial of service.
sections.eli5: Keys must be long enough, the numbers that make them unique must be random, and the office must check who you are before it does any work.
